items.scenarioContext: A friend is unusually quiet after receiving disappointing news.
items.prompt: What could you say?

options.text: “You should stop worrying.”
“You seem quieter than usual. Would you like to talk, or would you prefer some space?”
“I will tell everyone so they can cheer you up.”

a.feedback: This dismisses the feeling your friend may be sitting with. Noticing comes before fixing.

b.feedback: You name what you notice and leave the choice with your friend, which respects that they may not want to talk.

c.feedback: Sharing news they told you privately takes the decision away from them. Ask before involving other people.

items.followUpReflection: Which clues tell you a friend wants space instead of a conversation?

items.scenarioContext: A teammate makes a mistake and apologizes. You feel frustrated because the mistake caused extra work.
items.prompt: What is a constructive response?

options.text: “Thanks for acknowledging it. Let's review what needs fixing and how to prevent it next time.”
“You always ruin everything.”
“It is fine,” while refusing to discuss the impact.

a.feedback: You acknowledge the apology, name the practical impact, and move to a concrete next step. Naming your frustration is allowed too.

b.feedback: An accusation about the person rather than the work makes the problem harder to fix.

c.feedback: Keeping the peace can feel safer, but the unresolved impact usually returns. A short, specific conversation is kinder to both of you.

items.followUpReflection: What is one sentence that names your frustration without blaming the person?

items.scenarioContext: Someone interrupts while you are explaining an idea.
items.prompt: What is a useful response?

options.text: “I would like to finish my thought, then I want to hear yours.”
“You never listen.”
Stop contributing without explanation.

a.feedback: A clear, respectful request keeps the conversation open and protects your turn to speak.

b.feedback: A sweeping judgement about the person invites defence instead of change.

c.feedback: Stepping back can be right when a conversation is unsafe or disrespectful, but here nobody knows why you left. Say what you need first.

items.followUpReflection: What would you say if the same interruption happened again?

items.scenarioContext: A friend asks to borrow something you need today.
items.prompt: What can you do?

options.text: Say yes even though you cannot spare it.
Say, “I need it today, so I cannot lend it now.”
Hide the item and pretend you lost it.

a.feedback: Agreeing while you need the item today usually creates a second problem later. Kindness does not require saying yes.

b.feedback: A short, honest boundary without over-explaining. You can still offer another time if you want to.

c.feedback: Hiding the truth costs trust and still does not set a boundary.

items.followUpReflection: How would you offer a different day without weakening the boundary?

items.scenarioContext: You receive critical feedback in a meeting and feel defensive.
items.prompt: What is a constructive next step?

options.text: Ask for a specific example and listen before responding.
Criticize the colleague personally.
Agree with everything immediately, even if you do not understand.

a.feedback: Asking for an example slows the moment down and gives you real information to respond to. Disagreeing later is still allowed.

b.feedback: Turning feedback into a personal attack escalates the room and hides the actual concern.

c.feedback: Quick agreement may end the moment, but it abandons your own view and leaves the concern unresolved.

items.followUpReflection: What would help you pause for a few seconds before replying?

items.scenarioContext: A teammate misses a deadline. You do not know why.
items.prompt: What is a constructive first response?

options.text: Ask privately what blocked the work and discuss a realistic next step.
Assume they do not care.
Publicly shame them so others learn.

a.feedback: You look for context without dropping accountability, and you keep the conversation private.

b.feedback: The assumption fills in a reason you do not have and closes the conversation early.

c.feedback: Public shame damages trust and rarely improves the work.

items.followUpReflection: Which question would get you useful information without sounding like an interrogation?

items.scenarioContext: A friend has cancelled plans twice. You feel disappointed.
items.prompt: What could you do?

options.text: Explain how the cancellations affect you and ask whether the plan still works for them.
Pretend it does not matter, then resent them.
Send an insulting message.

a.feedback: You name the impact without accusing, and you invite information. Making other plans for yourself stays an option.

b.feedback: The feeling does not disappear just because it is unspoken; it usually grows.

c.feedback: An insult may release tension briefly, but it makes a repair much harder.

items.followUpReflection: What would you do with your evening if they cancel a third time?

items.scenarioContext: During a heated conversation, the other person demands an immediate answer. You feel overwhelmed and need time.
items.prompt: What is a constructive response?

options.text: “I want to discuss this, but I need 20 minutes to settle and think. I will come back at 3:00.”
Match their anger.
Leave indefinitely without communicating, even though it is safe to give an update.

a.feedback: You name the need, give a concrete time, and keep the commitment. If the situation is unsafe, leaving immediately and seeking help takes priority over any return time.

b.feedback: Raising the temperature usually escalates instead of resolving.

c.feedback: Space is legitimate, but silence leaves the other person guessing. One sentence is enough.

items.followUpReflection: How much time do you usually need before you can think clearly again?

items.scenarioContext: A colleague asks you to keep a secret, but the information suggests someone may be at risk of harm.
items.prompt: What should you consider?

options.text: Promise absolute secrecy.
Clarify the concern, avoid spreading the information, and seek appropriate help through a safe channel if someone may be at risk.
Post the details in a group chat.

a.feedback: An absolute promise can leave someone without help. You can respect privacy without promising something you may not be able to keep.

b.feedback: You keep the circle small, check what is actually known, and involve a safe, appropriate channel when safety is at stake. This is not legal or clinical advice.

c.feedback: Broadcasting details breaks trust and can put the person at more risk.

items.followUpReflection: Who is a safe person you could consult without spreading the details?

items.scenarioContext: A message in a group chat sounds rude, but tone is unclear and you lack context.
items.prompt: What is a thoughtful next step?

options.text: Publicly accuse the sender of being hostile.
Ask a neutral clarifying question or check privately before assuming intent.
Forward the message to others as proof.

a.feedback: A public accusation locks in an interpretation you cannot yet support.

b.feedback: You test your reading of the message before acting on it. If rudeness becomes a pattern, direct boundaries are still appropriate.

c.feedback: Spreading the message widens the conflict and adds people who were not part of it.

items.followUpReflection: What neutral question could you ask without sounding sarcastic?

items.scenarioContext: A teammate stops joking and goes quiet halfway through a meeting.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: You always go quiet when it matters.
You seem quieter than usual today. Is something on your mind?
Are you angry with me about something?

a.feedback: A generalised accusation rarely helps someone open up.

b.feedback: You name what you notice and leave it open for them to answer or not.

c.feedback: This jumps to blame and makes the moment about you.

items.followUpReflection: What small clue tells you a mood has shifted?

items.scenarioContext: A friend cancels plans twice in a row and replies with very few words.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: You are unreliable and I am done making plans.
I noticed you cancelled twice — is this a busy week, or is something else going on?
Fine, I will stop asking then.

a.feedback: A label shuts the conversation instead of opening it.

b.feedback: You check the pattern without assuming the reason.

c.feedback: This withdraws affection before you know what happened.

items.followUpReflection: How can you ask about a pattern without accusing?

items.scenarioContext: Your sister says she is fine but keeps sighing and avoids eye contact.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: You are clearly not fine, so stop pretending.
I hear "fine", but you look tired. Do you want to talk, or would rest help more?
If you say fine, I will drop it.

a.feedback: Calling it pretending can make her defend herself instead of sharing.

b.feedback: You name two signals without insisting on a single explanation, and offer options.

c.feedback: This accepts the surface answer and quietly leaves her alone.

items.followUpReflection: What does the mismatch between words and body language suggest?

items.scenarioContext: A colleague whose messages are usually warm sends a one-line, blunt reply.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I will answer in the same tone and see how they like it.
Your messages sound shorter today — did something happen, or was that just a rushed moment?
Why are you being rude all of a sudden?

a.feedback: Matching a tone you have not understood turns a blip into a conflict.

b.feedback: You test a guess instead of asserting one, and allow for a mundane cause.

c.feedback: Reading rudeness into one message escalates before you know anything.

items.followUpReflection: How much can one short message tell you?

items.scenarioContext: A friend jokes about failing an exam, then quickly changes the subject.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: You should have studied more and you know it.
You are making light of it — does it actually bother you more than it sounds?
At least you can laugh about it.

a.feedback: Adding blame to a raw moment rarely helps anyone reflect.

b.feedback: You notice the joke may be protecting something and invite the real feeling.

c.feedback: This rewards the deflection and closes the door on the feeling.

items.followUpReflection: Why might someone joke about a disappointment?

items.scenarioContext: Your partner goes quiet right after you mention an upcoming work trip.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: You went quiet when I mentioned the trip. What is coming up for you?
Do you not want me to go?
You always make simple things difficult.

a.feedback: You connect the silence to the moment and ask openly instead of guessing.

b.feedback: A yes-or-no question can feel like an accusation and invites defence.

c.feedback: A sweeping judgement hides the specific feeling under it.

items.followUpReflection: Which moment did the mood change at?

items.scenarioContext: You are tired, and a friend keeps returning to the same worry for the fourth time.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I have already heard this.
You always do this and then wonder why nobody listens.
I want to listen, and I am running low today. Can we take ten minutes now, or talk tomorrow when I can focus?

a.feedback: This states a limit but gives the friend nothing to work with.

b.feedback: It turns a limit into a character judgement and will likely shame them.

c.feedback: You name your own state and still offer a real choice, so honesty does not become rejection.

items.followUpReflection: How do you name your own limit without dismissing theirs?

items.scenarioContext: A teammate jokes about your mistake in front of the group, and you feel stung.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Very funny. Whatever.
Say it again and see what happens.
That landed badly for me. I would rather we talk about the mistake privately.

a.feedback: This hides the hurt and leaves the pattern to repeat.

b.feedback: A threat raises the stakes and shifts attention away from the behaviour.

c.feedback: You name the impact without attacking, and redirect to a setting that works.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want to happen next, not just now?

items.scenarioContext: A friend says "I am fine" in a flat voice after an argument at home.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: You are lying to me.
That did not sound fine. I am here if you want to talk, and it is okay if you do not.
Okay, if you are sure.

a.feedback: Accusing someone of lying pushes them to defend rather than share.

b.feedback: You reflect the mismatch, offer presence, and leave the choice with them.

c.feedback: This takes the words at face value and steps away from the moment.

items.followUpReflection: What does a flat voice add to the words?

items.scenarioContext: Someone you supervise looks close to tears during a review meeting.
items.prompt: What could you say or do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Let us finish quickly and move on.
Crying will not change the feedback.
Let us pause here. Would you like a short break, or to continue somewhere private?

a.feedback: Speeding up protects the agenda and ignores the person in front of you.

b.feedback: This frames the feeling as an obstacle and adds shame on top of it.

c.feedback: You notice the state, lower the pressure, and let them choose the setting.

items.followUpReflection: What does the meeting need to do for the person right now?

items.scenarioContext: You open a message that annoys you, and your thumb is already on reply.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Wait ten minutes, then reply once the heat has dropped.
Reply now, but keep it short.
Send the angry reply immediately.

a.feedback: A short pause usually changes what you are able to say.

b.feedback: Speed keeps the reaction in charge, even with fewer words.

c.feedback: Acting on the first surge tends to create a second problem.

items.followUpReflection: What could ten minutes change?

items.scenarioContext: You realise you will miss a deadline you agreed to.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Blame the tools and the workload.
Say so early, with a realistic new time.
Say nothing and hope nobody notices.

a.feedback: Blame protects your image at the expense of the relationship.

b.feedback: Early honesty gives the other person room to plan.

c.feedback: Silence shifts the cost to whoever was waiting.

items.followUpReflection: What does the other person need in order to plan?

items.scenarioContext: A meeting runs past the hour and you feel your focus fading.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Snap at the next person who speaks.
Ask for a short break, or suggest finishing in five minutes.
Silently scroll your phone.

a.feedback: Irritability lands on whoever happens to speak next.

b.feedback: Naming the limit early keeps the meeting and your attention usable.

c.feedback: Scrolling hides the problem and divides your attention.

items.followUpReflection: How can you change the situation before it changes your mood?

items.scenarioContext: You lose a game you expected to win.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Say the game was rigged.
Take a few slow breaths before analysing what happened.
Replay the loss angrily in your head for the rest of the evening.

a.feedback: Blaming the game avoids the part you could improve.

b.feedback: Lowering the heat first makes the analysis useful.

c.feedback: Rumination keeps the frustration alive without adding information.

items.followUpReflection: What would make the next game different?

items.scenarioContext: You feel a strong urge to check your phone while someone is telling you something important.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Keep scrolling while they talk.
Put the phone away and say you want to give them your attention.
Check it quickly, then apologise.

a.feedback: Half-listening is often felt, even when nothing is said.

b.feedback: Naming the intention makes the choice visible and easy to keep.

c.feedback: A quick check still splits the moment they asked you to share.

items.followUpReflection: What does the other person see while you decide?

items.scenarioContext: Two people give you opposite instructions and both expect theirs first.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Ask them to agree which comes first, and say you will follow that.
Do whichever is easier first.
Tell each one that the other is wrong.

a.feedback: You return the decision to the people who own the conflict.

b.feedback: Picking quietly leaves the conflict waiting for the next task.

c.feedback: Playing both sides against each other adds a third problem.

items.followUpReflection: Who actually owns this conflict?

items.scenarioContext: You are exhausted after a bad week, and a friend needs support tonight.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Say honestly what you can offer now, and when you can give more.
Agree to everything and resent it later.
Cancel without a word.

a.feedback: An honest, bounded offer is more reliable than an unlimited promise.

b.feedback: Overcommitting turns care into quiet resentment.

c.feedback: Silence leaves them without information or support.

items.followUpReflection: What can you actually give tonight?

items.scenarioContext: You feel unfairly blamed in a group chat and want to set the record straight.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Wait, then send one factual message without attacking anyone.
Answer every message as it arrives.
Screenshot the messages and mock the sender.

a.feedback: One clear, factual message is easier to answer than a stream of reactions.

b.feedback: Answering in real time keeps you inside the surge.

c.feedback: Mocking turns a dispute into a public conflict.

items.followUpReflection: What would a calm reader need to understand?

items.scenarioContext: A close friend cancels on you for the third time and you feel hurt.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Send a list of everything they have done wrong.
Name the pattern calmly and ask what is really happening.
Pretend it does not matter.

a.feedback: A list of grievances usually produces defence, not repair.

b.feedback: Naming the pattern without blame makes an honest answer possible.

c.feedback: Hiding the hurt lets it build into distance.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want to know, and what do you want to change?

items.scenarioContext: Someone makes a joke at your expense and you want to keep the mood light.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Leave the room without a word.
Laugh, then say honestly that one landed a bit close.
Laugh harder than you feel.

a.feedback: Walking out ends the moment without giving anyone information.

b.feedback: You keep the tone friendly and still tell the truth about the impact.

c.feedback: The extra laughter teaches people the joke is fine.

items.followUpReflection: How can a mood stay light while the message stays honest?

items.scenarioContext: A classmate snaps at you when you ask to borrow a pen.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They are just a bad person.
Something else may be going on; I will ask later.
They clearly hate me.

a.feedback: A character judgement ends the search for what happened.

b.feedback: Their reaction may belong to a different problem, so you leave room for that.

c.feedback: One sharp moment is thin evidence for a conclusion about you.

items.followUpReflection: What other explanation fits the same moment?

items.scenarioContext: A friend is late again and has not sent a message.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They do not respect my time at all.
I will leave and stop replying to them.
They may be dealing with something unexpected; I will ask when they arrive.

a.feedback: A general judgement about respect goes far beyond the evidence.

b.feedback: Leaving without a word punishes a story you have not checked.

c.feedback: Allowing for an unexpected cause keeps the question open.

items.followUpReflection: What would you need to know before deciding what the lateness means?

items.scenarioContext: Someone disagrees with your plan in a meeting.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They want to embarrass me in front of the team.
They never support anything I suggest.
They may see a risk I have not considered.

a.feedback: Intent to embarrass is an assumption, not something they said.

b.feedback: A pattern claim turns one moment into a verdict about them.

c.feedback: Disagreement often carries information worth reading.

items.followUpReflection: What would you learn by asking about their concern?

items.scenarioContext: A neighbour walks past without greeting you in the corridor.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They are doing it on purpose.
They may not have seen me, or may be distracted.
They are being rude.

a.feedback: Assuming intent turns an accident into a slight.

b.feedback: A missed greeting has several ordinary explanations.

c.feedback: Rudeness is one reading of many, and the least generous.

items.followUpReflection: Which explanations do not require anyone to be hostile?

items.scenarioContext: A friend cancels your plans and then posts about seeing other people.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They may need different kinds of time; I can say what I would like from the friendship.
They rank me last and everyone should know it.
I will cancel on them next time and see how they like it.

a.feedback: You allow for their reasons and still name your own wish.

b.feedback: A ranking claim turns a disappointment into a public verdict.

c.feedback: Retaliation creates a second grievance instead of a conversation.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want from this friendship, apart from this moment?

items.scenarioContext: Your parent questions almost every choice you make lately.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They may be worried rather than controlling; I will ask what worries them.
They want to run my life.
They do not care about me at all.

a.feedback: Naming worry instead of control tests a kinder explanation first.

b.feedback: Control may be part of it, but the intent is still a guess.

c.feedback: Indifference does not fit the effort of questioning everything.

items.followUpReflection: What feeling would explain the questions?

items.scenarioContext: A friend stops replying right after you share good news.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They were never a real friend.
They may be busy, or find the news hard right now; I will ask before assuming.
They are jealous and it shows.

a.feedback: One silence cannot carry the weight of a whole friendship verdict.

b.feedback: You hold two ordinary explanations open and check instead of concluding.

c.feedback: Jealousy is possible but reading it as proven skips the asking.

items.followUpReflection: What else was happening in their life this week?

items.scenarioContext: Someone you disagree with online writes a long, angry reply.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They are incapable of thinking clearly.
Something in my message may have felt dismissive; I will ask what landed badly.
They are just trolling for attention.

a.feedback: An ability claim is both unkind and untestable.

b.feedback: You consider your own contribution before assigning motive.

c.feedback: Trolling is one possibility, and it ends the inquiry early.

items.followUpReflection: Which part of your message could read differently than you meant?

items.scenarioContext: A friend keeps interrupting your story.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Can I finish this bit, then I want to hear yours?
You always interrupt me.
Forget it, then.

a.feedback: You ask for the space you need and keep the door open for them.

b.feedback: A pattern claim makes one moment into a complaint about them.

c.feedback: Withdrawing punishes them without saying what you wanted.

items.followUpReflection: What would let both of you speak?

items.scenarioContext: You need something from a colleague who is already busy.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I will tell our manager that you are blocking me.
Can you send that by Thursday? If not, tell me what is realistic.
Send it now, please.

a.feedback: Escalating before asking makes the request a threat.

b.feedback: You state the need and the timing, and leave room for their reality.

c.feedback: A bare demand ignores the workload you already know about.

items.followUpReflection: What does the other person need to answer well?

items.scenarioContext: A neighbour plays loud music late at night.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Leave an angry note on their door.
Hi, the music carries into my flat after eleven. Could you lower it then?
Turn it down or I will complain.

a.feedback: A note without a conversation is easy to dismiss.

b.feedback: You describe the specific effect and ask for a specific change.

c.feedback: A threat invites a fight rather than a fix.

items.followUpReflection: What exactly do you want to change, and when?

items.scenarioContext: A decision that affects you was made without you in the room.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Do whatever you want, then.
I would like to understand the reasoning, and share what I saw before we settle it.
That decision makes no sense.

a.feedback: Withdrawing leaves the decision and the resentment in place.

b.feedback: You ask for the reasoning and offer your view without demanding a reversal.

c.feedback: A flat dismissal invites defence and closes the discussion.

items.followUpReflection: What would you want them to know that they could not have known?

items.scenarioContext: A friend asks for feedback on writing that needs real work.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: It is fine, I guess.
It is bad. Start again.
Here is one thing that works, and the single change that would help most.

a.feedback: Vague reassurance leaves them unable to improve.

b.feedback: A verdict without direction is discouraging and unhelpful.

c.feedback: Specific, bounded feedback is usable and keeps the relationship intact.

items.followUpReflection: What is the one change that would matter most?

items.scenarioContext: You need to say no to a request without damaging the relationship.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Ask someone else, I am not doing it.
I cannot take this on now. I could help next week if it is still open.
I am too busy.

a.feedback: A flat refusal reads as rejection of the person, not the task.

b.feedback: You refuse clearly and keep a real option on the table.

c.feedback: A reason without a boundary leaves the request technically open.

items.followUpReflection: What can you offer that is true?

items.scenarioContext: Two colleagues blame each other in a meeting you are chairing.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Let them finish and hope it resolves itself.
Tell the group which of them is clearly at fault.
Let us pause, restate both concerns, and agree one next step with an owner.

a.feedback: Hoping leaves the conflict to grow and the meeting without an outcome.

b.feedback: Taking a side turns a work problem into a loyalty contest.

c.feedback: You slow the exchange, name both concerns, and move to an actionable step.

items.followUpReflection: What would let the meeting end with one clear next action?

items.scenarioContext: You must give critical feedback to someone who reports to you.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Say it generally so it stings less.
Save it for the review and list everything at once.
Describe the specific behaviour and its effect, then agree what changes.

a.feedback: Generality protects the giver and leaves the receiver guessing.

b.feedback: A stored list arrives as a verdict and is hard to use.

c.feedback: Specific behaviour plus agreed change is feedback someone can act on.

items.followUpReflection: What could they do differently next week?

items.scenarioContext: A friend repeats a joke about you that has started to hurt.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Just stop joking with me altogether.
Fine. I will remember that.
I know it is a joke, and it is landing badly for me now. Can we drop that one?

a.feedback: A blanket rule costs the friendship more than the joke does.

b.feedback: A veiled threat keeps the hurt and adds distance.

c.feedback: You name the shift honestly, keep goodwill, and ask for one specific change.

items.followUpReflection: What exactly do you want them to stop?

items.scenarioContext: You realise mid-argument that you were partly wrong.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Say which part you got wrong, and what you still see differently.
Change the subject before it gets worse.

Let the gap open and keep your speed steady.
Lean on the horn for a long time.

a.feedback: Tailgating turns anger into danger.

b.feedback: Steady driving keeps the risk low and the feeling manageable.

c.feedback: A long horn expresses the surge and adds risk.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want to be true two minutes from now?

items.scenarioContext: Your food arrives wrong after a long wait.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Eat it and post a complaint later.
Refuse to pay and raise your voice.
Tell the server calmly what you ordered and ask them to fix it.

a.feedback: Eating it hides the error and leaves the frustration to grow.

b.feedback: Escalating over a wrong dish costs more than the dish.

c.feedback: A calm, specific request usually gets the order fixed.

items.followUpReflection: What outcome would make this evening fine?

items.scenarioContext: A close friend points out a habit you dislike hearing about.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Let me tell you about one of your flaws first.
Can you give me an example? I want to sit with it before I answer.
Let us talk about something else.

a.feedback: Counter-attacking makes the conversation about scorekeeping.

b.feedback: Asking for an example buys time and turns the sting into information.

c.feedback: Changing the subject protects you and loses the feedback.

items.followUpReflection: What would you want to know before reacting?

items.scenarioContext: You receive a short, blunt rejection for a job you wanted.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Wait an hour, then ask for one line of feedback.
Reply at once asking why they rejected you.
Send a long email explaining what they got wrong.

a.feedback: A short pause keeps the request for feedback likely to be answered.

b.feedback: An immediate reply usually carries the sting into the wording.

c.feedback: A long rebuttal closes the door on any future contact.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want from them a week from now?

items.scenarioContext: A meeting blames you for a delay another team caused.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I will say nothing and let it stand.
I want to correct one thing: the delay came from the handover. Here is what I can do next.
I will list everything the other team did wrong.

a.feedback: Silence makes the record permanent.

b.feedback: You correct the record once, without blame, and move to action.

c.feedback: A list of the other team shifts blame without fixing the delay.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want the room to conclude, and what do you want done?

items.scenarioContext: You have written a message while furious and your finger is on send.
items.prompt: What is the most useful next step?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Save it as a draft and read it again tomorrow.
Send it and apologise later.
Send it and block them.

a.feedback: A draft keeps your points and removes the heat.

b.feedback: Sending costs trust that an apology may not restore.

c.feedback: Blocking makes the conflict permanent.

items.followUpReflection: What part of this message would you still stand by tomorrow?

items.scenarioContext: Someone in a queue waves you ahead without saying anything.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They are planning something.
They may simply be in less of a hurry than I am.
They think I am weak.

a.feedback: Suspicion turns kindness into a threat.

b.feedback: The simplest explanation needs no hidden motive.

c.feedback: This reads a judgement about you into a small courtesy.

items.followUpReflection: Which explanation needs the fewest assumptions?

items.scenarioContext: A classmate disagrees with you in almost every discussion.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: They hate me personally.
They just want attention.
They may enjoy testing ideas; I can ask what they think is strongest.

a.feedback: Personal dislike is a guess the discussions do not establish.

b.feedback: Attention-seeking dismisses the content of what they say.

c.feedback: Curiosity about their reasoning turns friction into exchange.

items.followUpReflection: What might they be getting from the debate?

items.scenarioContext: A colleague asks for a deadline extension for the second time this month.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Something in their workload may be changing; I will ask before deciding.
They are simply disorganised.
I will refuse and copy their manager.

a.feedback: Asking first keeps the decision fair and may reveal a real constraint.

b.feedback: A trait explanation skips the question of what changed.

c.feedback: Escalating before asking turns a scheduling issue into a record.

items.followUpReflection: What would you need to know to decide fairly?

items.scenarioContext: A friend forgets your birthday for the first time in years.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I will forget theirs on purpose.
One missed date may not mean less care; I will say it matters to me.
They never really cared.

a.feedback: Retaliation replaces the conversation with a quiet contest.

b.feedback: You separate one lapse from the whole history and state your need.

c.feedback: A verdict about years of care from one date is a big leap.

items.followUpReflection: What would you want them to know about how this felt?

items.scenarioContext: A teammate praises the team publicly but complains about you privately.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I will stop contributing until they admit it.
Both may be true at once: they value the outcome and find the process hard.
They are two-faced and everyone should know.

a.feedback: Withdrawing punishes the work and hides the issue.

b.feedback: Holding two truths keeps you from flattening them into a villain.

c.feedback: A public label removes any chance of an honest conversation.

items.followUpReflection: What would you want to hear from them directly?

items.scenarioContext: Your sibling is unusually generous right before asking for something.
items.prompt: What is most likely going on for them?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Generosity and a request can coexist; I will hear the request without assuming manipulation.
They want something, as always.

a.feedback: You stay open to both motives and let the request stand on its own.

b.feedback: Assuming the worst makes the conversation about your suspicion.

items.followUpReflection: What would change if you heard the request first?

items.scenarioContext: You need to leave a long meeting early.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I need to leave at three. Can we cover my item before then?
Slip out quietly when nobody is looking.
Interrupt and announce that you are done.

a.feedback: You give the timing and a workable request.

b.feedback: Leaving quietly leaves your item undiscussed.

c.feedback: Announcing an exit interrupts everyone without solving your item.

items.followUpReflection: What needs to happen before you go?

items.scenarioContext: A friend asks how your week was, but you have two minutes.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Busy, and I want to tell you properly — can we talk tonight?
Fine, whatever.
Ignore the message.

a.feedback: You name the limit and offer a real time.

b.feedback: A flat answer closes the conversation they opened.

c.feedback: Silence reads as disinterest.

items.followUpReflection: What would you want if you were them?

items.scenarioContext: You disagree with a friend's plan for a trip you are taking together.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I want this trip to work for both of us. Can we list what each of us needs?
Your plan is too expensive.
I will book separately and tell you later.

a.feedback: You frame the shared goal and invite both sets of needs.

b.feedback: A verdict on the plan invites defence instead of adjustment.

c.feedback: Booking separately ends the shared trip without a conversation.

items.followUpReflection: What does each of you actually need from this trip?

items.scenarioContext: A colleague's meeting runs over and you have the room booked next.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Stand by the door and sigh loudly.
Start your meeting over theirs.
We have the room booked from four. Could we take it in ten minutes?

a.feedback: Sighing asks them to guess what you need.

b.feedback: Taking the room escalates a scheduling problem into a conflict.

c.feedback: A specific, polite request usually resolves a booking clash.

items.followUpReflection: What is the smallest request that solves this?

items.scenarioContext: You have to tell a friend you cannot attend their wedding.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I want to tell you early, in person: I cannot be there. Here is what I can do instead.
Send a message the week before.
Say nothing and let them find out.

a.feedback: Early, direct news lets them plan and shows the relationship matters.

b.feedback: Late news limits their options and feels like avoidance.

c.feedback: Silence leaves them to discover it themselves.

items.followUpReflection: What would you want if the roles were reversed?

items.scenarioContext: You need to raise a sensitive issue with a whole group, not one person.
items.prompt: What could you say?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Send a long message listing each person's part.
I want to raise something once, hear how others see it, and agree how we decide.
Hint at it until someone else says it out loud.

a.feedback: A list of individual faults turns a group issue into a trial.

b.feedback: Naming the process first makes a hard topic safer to discuss.

c.feedback: Hinting leaves the issue unnamed and the group guessing.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want the group to be able to do afterwards?

items.scenarioContext: A neighbour asks to borrow your tools every weekend.
items.prompt: What could you do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I keep my tools for my own work; there is a shop nearby that lends them.
Say yes and hide the tools next time.
Lend them and complain to other neighbours.

a.feedback: A clear no with an alternative keeps the relationship workable.

b.feedback: Hiding avoids the request and creates a strange game.

c.feedback: Lending while resenting turns a favour into a grievance.

items.followUpReflection: What do you want the next request to look like?

items.scenarioContext: Someone invites you to an event on your only rest day.
items.prompt: What could you do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Agree and cancel on the day.
I am not available that day. I hope it goes well.
Maybe, I will decide later.

a.feedback: Cancelling on the day costs them more than an early no.

b.feedback: A short no leaves the rest day intact and respects them.

c.feedback: A vague maybe keeps you both waiting.

items.followUpReflection: What does your rest day need from you?

items.scenarioContext: A coworker asks for your home address to send a gift.
items.prompt: What could you do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Give the address and feel uneasy about it.
Send it to the office; that is the address I use for work things.

a.feedback: Sharing to avoid awkwardness leaves you uncomfortable.

b.feedback: You offer a workable alternative without sharing more than you want.

items.followUpReflection: What is the smallest thing that solves their need?

items.scenarioContext: A friend asks you to pass messages between them and someone you are also close to.
items.prompt: What could you do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: I care about you both. I can listen, but I will not carry messages between you.
Pass the messages and hope it settles.

a.feedback: You keep care and refuse the role that would put you in the middle.

b.feedback: Carrying messages makes you responsible for an outcome you cannot control.

items.followUpReflection: What role can you hold without losing either friendship?

items.scenarioContext: Your team expects replies in a group chat after working hours.
items.prompt: What could you do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Mute the group and hope nobody notices.
Keep replying at midnight and resent it.
I check the group during work hours; anything urgent should be a call.

a.feedback: Muting hides the boundary instead of setting it.

b.feedback: Late replies teach the team that evenings are available.

c.feedback: You state the channel for urgency and keep the boundary visible.

items.followUpReflection: How would people reach you if something were genuinely urgent?

items.scenarioContext: A family member expects weekly visits you cannot sustain.
items.prompt: What could you do?
items.instructions: There is no single perfect answer; pick the response you could actually use.

options.text: Stop visiting and explain later.
Visit every week and burn out quietly.
I can come every other week, and I can call on the weeks I am not there.

a.feedback: Disappearing without explanation strains the relationship more.

b.feedback: Weekly visits at the cost of exhaustion end in a sudden stop anyway.

c.feedback: A concrete rhythm keeps the relationship and your capacity.

items.followUpReflection: What rhythm could you keep for a year?
